binding_instruments.rationale: No AI-specific binding instrument exists, and no general data protection statute is in force that could be applied to AI.

economic_tools.rationale: The only AI-linked public investment is a World Bank-supported pilot classifying buildings and rooftops under the Caribbean Digital Transformation Project, with no sandbox or AI procurement rules.

institutional_capacity.rationale: No ministry unit, council or agency in Dominica holds an AI mandate, advisory or statutory.

soft_law.rationale: No national AI guidance, ethics document, code or standard has been published by any Dominican ministry or regulator.

ai_specificity.rationale: Dominica has not enacted comprehensive data protection legislation, and the Electronic Evidence Act 2010 and Credit Reporting Act 2020 contain no AI provisions.

binding_force.rationale: No AI statute, bill or binding rule exists in Dominica; the Cullen International September 2026 Caribbean review records no AI regulation for the country.

implementation.rationale: The only adjacent instrument, the National Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026, is a paper framework with no AI obligations or implementing rules.

scope.rationale: No sector, use case or public-sector AI activity is covered by any binding Dominican rule.

academia.rationale: The Senate committee heard the Instituto Tecnológico de las Américas (ITLA) director on the AI bill and universities contributed to the ENIA, with no permanent advisory seat.

civil_society.rationale: Civil society joined the Open Government Partnership-supported co-creation of the AI Ethics Code and ENIA consultations on an episodic basis.

industry.rationale: Industry took part in ENIA consultations, the participatory workshops behind the draft AI Ethics Code and Senate committee hearings, without standing statutory roles.

international.rationale: The country hosted the Third Ministerial Summit on AI Ethics in Latin America and the Caribbean in Santo Domingo in June 2026 and works through UNESCO, Red GEALC and PARLATINO.

actions_taken.rationale: No prosecution or decision under the AI content offences of Ley 74-25 has been published since they took effect on 3 August 2026.

dedicated_authority.rationale: Enforcement falls to the Ministerio Público and ordinary courts under the Penal Code; no authority holds an explicit AI remit.

monitoring_practice.rationale: Monitoring is limited to ENIA action-plan progress reporting by OGTIC; no AI audit or supervision programme operates.

sanctions_framework.rationale: Ley 74-25 sets prison terms of up to ten years for AI-generated intimate or deceptive content; no administrative penalties exist for any other AI obligation.

formal_coordination.rationale: Decreto 338-23 created the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital and Decreto 498-23 obliges executive entities to coordinate AI projects through it.

nongovernmental_checks.rationale: No court ruling, ombudsman action or independent review body addressing AI has been recorded in the Dominican Republic.

regulator_plurality.rationale: OGTIC under the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital leads AI policy, with DIGEIG and the Ministerio de Administración Pública contributing public-sector ethics but no sectoral AI regulators.

subnational_role.rationale: Municipalities and provinces hold no AI regulatory or implementing role; all AI instruments are national.

institutional_capacity.rationale: OGTIC and the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital hold AI coordination mandates under Decreto 498-23 and Decreto 338-23 without compliance powers or dedicated enforcement staff.

soft_law.rationale: Published soft law consists of the ENIA and the DIGEIG draft National AI Ethics Code, announced in June 2026 for approval by decree and not yet promulgated.

ai_specificity.rationale: AI is addressed expressly inside adapted general law (Ley 74-25 Penal Code articles on AI-generated content) rather than in a dedicated AI statute.

binding_force.rationale: Ley 74-25 (Código Penal), in force 3 August 2026, criminalises AI-altered intimate or false content, the sole binding AI rule, covering one use case.

implementation.rationale: Beyond the penal articles, Decreto 498-23 and the ENIA carry no implementing rules, and no competent AI authority has been designated.

scope.rationale: Binding coverage is limited to AI-generated or AI-altered intimate and deceptive content under Ley 74-25; no sectoral AI duties exist.

academia.rationale: Academic representatives attended the 2025 UNESCO readiness workshops, holding no advisory role in AI policy.

civil_society.rationale: Civil society participated only in the one-off UNESCO readiness workshops of 8-9 April and 27 May 2025.

industry.rationale: Private-sector input came through Catalpa International's delivery role in the 2025 readiness assessment, with no standing industry consultation channel.

international.rationale: Timor-Leste endorsed the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, attended the 2025 AI Action Summit in Paris and spoke at a UN Group of Friends AI capacity-building briefing…

actions_taken.rationale: No AI enforcement action has been taken by any Timorese authority.

dedicated_authority.rationale: No authority holds an AI enforcement remit, and Timor-Leste has no data protection authority either.

monitoring_practice.rationale: The only oversight output is the one-off 2025 UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology country report.

sanctions_framework.rationale: No AI obligation exists, so no penalty is defined in Timorese law.

formal_coordination.rationale: Coordination occurs through one-off projects and events such as the UNESCO readiness workshops and the August 2026 Government Dialogue, with no standing mechanism.

nongovernmental_checks.rationale: No court ruling, ombudsman action or independent review body has addressed AI in Timor-Leste.

regulator_plurality.rationale: AI matters rest with central government, principally the Ministry of Transport and Communications and TIC Timor, with no sectoral regulator holding an AI remit.

subnational_role.rationale: Municipalities have no role in AI policy, which is handled entirely by national ministries.

binding_instruments.rationale: No binding AI instrument exists, and Timor-Leste has no general data protection statute through which AI could be bindingly regulated.

economic_tools.rationale: No AI funding programme, AI procurement rule or regulatory sandbox has been established.

institutional_capacity.rationale: AI work sits with the Ministry of Transport and Communications and TIC Timor, neither of which holds a legal AI mandate.

implementation.rationale: Only paper commitments exist: Timor Digital 2032 and the 2025 UNESCO readiness report, with no implementing rule or competent authority.

scope.rationale: No sector, use case or public-sector AI obligation is covered by any binding Timorese instrument.

industry.rationale: Industry takes part in the Comité de Inteligencia Artificial, SPDP public consultations on draft resolutions and Comisión de Educación hearings, without a standing decision role.

industry.rationale: Industry holds standing seats on the NCAI and participated in consultations on the March 2026 governance framework, without a formal role in drafting binding rules.

formal_coordination.rationale: Coordination rests on joint issuances such as DICT-CSC JMC No. 003 and inter-agency consultations rather than a statutory AI council.

nongovernmental_checks.rationale: No court ruling or independent review body has shaped AI rules; oversight comes from NPC advisories and congressional hearings.

regulator_plurality.rationale: DICT, CSC, DOST/NAICRI, DEPDev, NPC, BSP, CHED and COMELEC each act on AI within their own remits, with no statutory lead AI regulator.

subnational_role.rationale: Local government units apply national issuances on government AI use but adopt no AI rules of their own.

binding_instruments.rationale: Two AI-specific binding issuances are in force: COMELEC Resolution No. 11064 (2024) and DICT-CSC Joint Memorandum Circular No. 003, Series of 2026.

economic_tools.rationale: Funding flows through CAIR, NAICRI, the National AI Center and the AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan 2026-2033, with no operating AI regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rules.

institutional_capacity.rationale: DICT, DEPDev, NAICRI and the National AI Center carry AI mandates administratively, none holding statutory AI compliance powers pending the bill creating an AI authority.

soft_law.rationale: Guidance spans the National AI Strategy for the Philippines (2025), NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 and BSP Memoranda M-2026-031 and M-2026-034, without national AI technical standards.

ai_specificity.rationale: Dedicated AI-specific issuances exist for elections, government use and NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 on the Data Privacy Act, but none governs AI systems generally.

binding_force.rationale: No AI statute is enacted; binding AI rules in force cover only election campaign content (COMELEC Resolution No. 11064) and government AI use (DICT-CSC JMC No. 003, s. 2026).

implementation.rationale: COMELEC Resolution No. 11064 was applied in the 2025 national, local and BARMM elections and JMC No. 003 took effect 9 June 2026, but no horizontal AI framework is in force.

scope.rationale: Coverage is limited to one content type (election campaign material) and to public-sector AI use, with no binding obligations on private-sector high-risk AI.

academia.rationale: NASK and university consortia build the PLLuM models and academics advised on the draft AI Systems Act, without a standing statutory seat.

civil_society.rationale: NGOs took part in public consultations on the AI Systems Act, while the statutory Social Council for Artificial Intelligence of 9 to 15 members is not yet appointed.

industry.rationale: Business was consulted on successive drafts of the AI Systems Act and the Policy for AI Development until 2030 and sits in the PL/AI group, but not on KRiBSI itself.

international.rationale: Poland signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, has not ratified it, and sits on the EU AI Board and in OECD AI work.

actions_taken.rationale: KRiBSI gained inspection and fining powers on 28 October 2026 and has issued no decision; only UODO has acted on AI under the GDPR.

dedicated_authority.rationale: KRiBSI is the designated national AI market surveillance authority with a chair, statutory budget and powers over part of the rules, while UODO covers data protection aspects.

monitoring_practice.rationale: KRiBSI has announced first supervisory priorities covering emotion recognition at work, CSAM tools and AI content labelling, with no audit or monitoring report published.

sanctions_framework.rationale: Administrative fines up to EUR 35 million or 7% of turnover are defined by the AI Act and Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1003 and applicable from 28 October 2026, except for deferred high-risk duties.

formal_coordination.rationale: The Act of 3 July 2026 builds coordination into KRiBSI's collegiate membership drawn from UOKiK, UKE, KNF and KRRiT, with a Social Council for AI attached but not yet constituted.

nongovernmental_checks.rationale: KRiBSI decisions are appealable to the Warsaw competition and consumer protection court and any person may lodge a complaint, with no AI ruling issued yet.

regulator_plurality.rationale: Market surveillance is centralised in KRiBSI as the single national AI authority, with UODO retaining separate GDPR oversight.

subnational_role.rationale: Poland is unitary and no voivodeship or municipal body holds any AI regulatory or implementing competence under Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1003.

binding_instruments.rationale: Two AI-specific binding instruments bind in Poland: the EU AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and the Act of 3 July 2026 on AI Systems.

economic_tools.rationale: The PLN 1 billion AI Fund, PLLuM language-model funding and PLN 35 million earmarked for the KRiBSI regulatory sandbox exist, but no sandbox is yet operating.

institutional_capacity.rationale: KRiBSI has a statutory AI mandate, a chair appointed 18 September 2026 and a PLN 9.3 million 2026 budget, but the collegiate Commission has not yet held its first sitting.

soft_law.rationale: UODO published AI initial-question checklists on 6 August 2026 and the Ministry of Digital Affairs published an AI guide for public administration on ai.gov.pl in 2026.

ai_specificity.rationale: The Act of 3 July 2026 on Artificial Intelligence Systems and the EU AI Act regulate AI systems and models generally, not through adapted general law.

binding_force.rationale: EU AI Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) and the Act of 3 July 2026 on AI Systems bind, but high-risk duties run from December 2027.

implementation.rationale: KRiBSI's inspection, complaint and penalty chapters apply from 28 October 2026, yet the Commission's first sitting is due by 11 November 2026 and no sandbox competition has opened.

implementation.rationale: ANACOM acts as market surveillance authority and single point of contact, while the national diploma on competent authorities and fines remained unpublished in October 2026.

scope.rationale: The AI Act covers all sectors by design, yet its high-risk obligations are not applicable until December 2027 and August 2028.

regulator_plurality.rationale: FZ-243 allocates powers to the Government, the Ministry of Digital Development, the Ministry of Economic Development for experimental regimes, the FSB and the Bank of Russia.

subnational_role.rationale: Moscow operates the AI experimental legal regime established by Federal Law No. 123-FZ and regions host regimes approved under FZ-258, implementing federal rules.

institutional_capacity.rationale: The Ministry of Digital Development and the Government hold statutory AI powers under FZ-243, none of which have been used as compliance powers before 1 March 2027.

soft_law.rationale: The National Code of Ethics in the Field of Artificial Intelligence (2021) with sectoral codes and Rosstandart technical committee 164 GOST standards cover several areas.

ai_specificity.rationale: FZ-243 is a dedicated AI statute defining artificial intelligence and large foundation models, with binding duties confined to that one class of models.

binding_force.rationale: Federal Law No. 243-FZ of 26 July 2026 is in force since 1 September 2026, but developer duties, labelling tools and copyright rules apply only from 1 March 2027.

implementation.rationale: FZ-243 is in a staged transition, with core obligations deferred to 1 March 2027 and to 2032 for deployed foreign systems, and implementing government acts not yet issued.

scope.rationale: FZ-243 regulates only large foundation models, excluding small models and machine-vision AI, alongside sector-specific experimental legal regimes under FZ-123 and FZ-258.

civil_society.rationale: Domestic civil society participated in the 2023 National AI Policy drafting consultations and has had no recurring role since.

industry.rationale: Industry contributed through policy drafting workshops, the ICT Chamber, C4IR Rwanda and the Rwanda AI Scaling Hub, without a standing statutory advisory seat.

international.rationale: Rwanda hosted the Global AI Summit on Africa, sponsored the Africa Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (2025), leads Smart Africa and addressed the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

monitoring_practice.rationale: Monitoring is limited to readiness measurement under the AI Readiness and Maturity Framework for Rwanda; no compliance audits of AI systems are conducted.

regulator_plurality.rationale: MINICT and the National Artificial Intelligence Agency lead, with RURA, the National Cyber Security Authority and the National Bank of Rwanda acting within existing sectoral remits.

subnational_role.rationale: Rwanda is a unitary state; districts and provinces hold no AI rule-making or implementation role in the National AI Policy.

binding_instruments.rationale: Only general law reaches AI: Law No. 058/2021 on personal data protection and Law No. 24/2016 governing ICT, neither containing AI-specific provisions.
